paras: The threatened lynching of Robert Porterfield took place in Montgomery, Alabama, in April 1919, after Porterfield, a Black man, shot police officer J. Earl Davis in a gunfight that began with Davis's arrest of Porterfield's wife. When a correspondent overheard white men discussing a possible lynching of the prisoner, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People appealed to Governor Thomas E. Kilby, who had Porterfield removed to Mobile for safe keeping. The NAACP publicized the governor's reply as a contrast to Mississippi governor Theodore G. Bilbo's response to the Shubuta lynchings.

On a Thursday afternoon, apparently April 10, Officer Davis was sent to quell a disturbance near Porterfield's store at the corner of Terry and Union streets. According to the New York Age's Montgomery report, Davis "is said to have placed Mrs. Porterfield under arrest" and was searching her when Porterfield arrived and objected to her treatment. A "duel with revolvers" followed, in which Davis shot Porterfield in the throat and the hand and Porterfield shot Davis through the skull, a wound the Age called "the fatal shot." Several hours later Porterfield surrendered at the county jail, saying he had shot in self defense.

The shooting stirred "ill feeling between the races," and the mayor and city council postponed a reception at the Auditorium for Black soldiers recently returned from overseas. A correspondent in Montgomery then reported to the NAACP that he had overheard "a group of white men discuss the possible lynching" of the prisoner.

On April 14 the NAACP, through its secretary John R. Shillady, wired Governor Kilby asking for an investigation and protection for the prisoner. Kilby replied on April 17 that the prisoner had been removed to Mobile for safe keeping and would have "all necessary protection." The coverage does not report Davis's death outright, nor any charge, trial or later fate for Porterfield.

The case appeared only in the Black press, in two forms. The New York Age ran a plain Montgomery report on its front page on April 19, attributing the arrest and search to hearsay and recording Porterfield's claim of self defense. A week later the NAACP's release on the governor's reply appeared in the Black Dispatch, in a badly garbled copy headed "NO 'TO HELL WITH 'EM' THIS TIME," and in the Wisconsin Weekly Blade. The release did not name Porterfield; it treated the case as a test of Southern governors, setting Kilby's protection against Bilbo's remark that he would tell the NAACP "to go to h——" about the Shubuta lynchings.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Robert Porterfield
bases: A Black prisoner who had shot a police officer was the subject of lynching talk among white men, and the governor had him removed to Mobile for protection (A3, A2); the coverage reports no mob attack, so this is at most a threatened lynching (A1, A3).

No one was killed by a mob: Porterfield was wounded by the officer in a gunfight, surrendered, and was moved to Mobile after white men were overheard discussing lynching him (A1, A3). The papers report talk of a lynching over his shooting of a policeman, not an attack.

The lynching talk rests on one NAACP release, from an unnamed correspondent, carried in two papers (A2, A3); the shooting and the race feeling it caused are reported separately only by the New York Age (A1).

accounts.label: Montgomery correspondent (New York Age)
accounts.gist: Officer Davis arrested and searched Mrs. Porterfield; Porterfield objected, a revolver duel followed, and each wounded the other; Porterfield surrendered and claimed self defense.

accounts.label: NAACP release
accounts.gist: A Montgomery correspondent overheard white men discussing a possible lynching of the man who shot a policeman; on the NAACP's appeal the governor had him moved to Mobile.

framing.detail: The New York Age reported the gunfight plainly, noting that Davis 'is said to' have been searching Mrs. Porterfield and giving Porterfield's self-defense claim, and tied the postponed soldiers' reception to 'ill feeling between the races.'
The NAACP release, headed in the Black Dispatch 'NO "TO HELL WITH 'EM" THIS TIME,' presented the governor's protection as a contrast to Bilbo's dismissal of the Shubuta lynchings.

record_check.dossier: Porterfield is the only target of anti-Black violence; J. Earl Davis was the police officer who shot him and whom he shot.
threatened: white men were overheard discussing a lynching; no mob gathered or moved on the jail in the coverage.
Shooting on a Thursday before April 14, apparently April 10; NAACP wire April 14; governor's reply April 17.
Shooting a police officer (Porterfield claimed self defense).
The shooting was a gunfight between Porterfield and the arresting officer; the lynching element was talk overheard, not an act.
Officer Davis was shot in the head ('the fatal shot'); his race is not stated and his death is implied, not reported outright.

record_check.record: prisoner was moved to a safe place
record_check.dossier: Moved to Mobile, Ala.; the prisoner had been wounded in a gunfight with an officer he shot.
